title: The Sleeping Winter
premise: Folklorist Lior Sandoval arrives in the snowbound village of Vell Hollow to record its winter songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any verse twice—and every photograph he takes now shows an extra chair at the hearth, one that wasn't there before. As the chair draws closer to the camera with each roll of film, Lior realizes the village's founders bound something beneath the harvest fields, a hunger fed by song and sustained by forgetting, and his documentation has been waking it. To survive, he must complete the founders' unfinished ritual before the harvest moon rises: sing the forbidden verses himself, twice, and take the empty chair as his own. He does—trading his name and memory for the village's safety—but the final photograph shows him seated by the fire, smiling, waiting for the next folklorist.
about_author: Xanthe Crane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing oral histories from disappearing rural communities before turning to horror. They write in unheated farmhouses and claim their best ideas arrive during power outages.

chapters.title: The Verse Nobody Repeats
chapters.summary: Lior arrives in Vell Hollow with recording equipment and academic confidence, welcomed warmly but warned subtly by innkeeper Marta Voss never to ask anyone to sing a song twice. His POV establishes his belief that documentation preserves what time erases. The emotional beat is uneasy hospitality—the village is kind the way a locked room is quiet.

chapters.title: Field Recordings
chapters.summary: Lior collects fragments of winter songs from elderly residents, noticing each singer stops mid-verse and refuses, with genuine terror, to continue. An old woman, Irena, hums a melody matching nothing in any archive. His POV; the beat is scholarly fascination curdling into the first real dread when a singer whispers, 'It remembers whoever repeats it.'

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Developing his photographs at grandma's rented house, Lior finds every image of the hearth includes an empty wooden chair that isn't physically there. Comparing rolls chronologically, the chair sits farther away in older photos and nearer in recent ones. His POV; the beat is rationalization collapsing—he measures the distance like a countdown.

chapters.title: What the Founders Buried
chapters.summary: In the church basement archive, Lior finds the founders' ledger: a ritual half-recorded, its final verses torn out, describing something fed by song and lulled by collective forgetting. Marta catches him reading and finally explains the rule. His POV; the beat is horrified comprehension—the village isn't cruel, it's terrified.

chapters.title: Irena's Confession
chapters.summary: Irena reveals she once sang a verse twice as a girl, and her brother vanished into the harvest fields that night; she has hummed the incomplete melody for sixty years trying to lure it back. Her POV briefly, then Lior's. The beat is grief weaponized into purpose—Irena asks Lior to finish what she started.

chapters.title: The Village Closes
chapters.summary: The harvest moon approaches; roads out are snowed shut, phones dead, and villagers begin gathering nightly to sing the safe verses in unison, louder each time, like a wall of sound. Lior realizes his recordings have been weakening the barrier. His POV; the beat is claustrophobic guilt—his prayer of documentation became an invitation.

chapters.title: Chair at the Table
chapters.summary: The chair appears physically now, moved each morning closer to Lior's bed, and villagers stop meeting his eyes—they can see it too, which means it has chosen him. Marta begs him to leave through the pass before moonrise. His POV; the beat is isolation sharpening into resolve: staying invisible was never an option, so he chooses to act.

chapters.title: The Torn Verses
chapters.summary: Lior and Irena reconstruct the missing ritual verses from her sixty years of humming, his recordings played backward, and the ledger's marginalia. The completed text requires a singer willing to be remembered by the thing below. His POV; the beat is terrible clarity—the ritual doesn't banish it, it feeds it a keeper.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: Under the rising moon, Lior walks into the frozen fields, sets up his recorder to document everything one last time, and sings the forbidden verses twice while the ground opens around the extra chair. The thing beneath rises—not monstrous but hungry and lonely, wearing the faces of everyone ever forgotten. His POV; the climax beat is courage as surrender.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Song
chapters.summary: Lior takes the chair and becomes the village's new forgotten one, his name erased from records and memories alike; Marta finds only his recorder, still warm, playing a melody no archive contains. Epilogue shifts to a young folklorist arriving next winter, drawn by a song she can't stop humming. The beat is chilling belonging—Lior got exactly what he wanted, forever.
